items.title: Secrets of Effective Upskilling
items.raw_text: This is an excerpt from Upskilling for Library Workers: A Guide for Future-Ready Professionals by Ann Medaille (ALA Editions, 2026). With the advent of new technologies and rapid social and economic shifts, library workers’ jobs are being transformed. Compared with a decade ago, library workers now spend more time consulting on complex research tools, teaching digital literacy classes, supporting virtual learning environments, helping users troubleshoot devices, and codesigning projects with community partners. The pace at which library staffers are called upon to learn new skills is accelerating, and workers may struggle to keep up. In addition, automation and artificial intelligence (AI) are altering many aspects of work. In the long run, technological innovations have the potential to increase productivity and lead to more interesting kinds of work, but in the short term, they often cause disruptions that can be difficult for workers to navigate. To address these changes—and manage the anxieties that come along with them—workers need constant support for skill development. While corporations may embrace upskilling to stay competitive, libraries will have to support upskilling to remain relevant. Library leaders are under greater pressure to respond rapidly to changing social and economic conditions and demonstrate that their libraries make a difference in their communities. items.title: Hold the Phone
items.raw_text: Since fall 2024, each school day at Grant High School in Portland, Oregon, has started the same way: Roughly 2,100 students line up to place their phones in gray and green Yondr pouches—the kind live performers use to prevent audience members from recording—as they enter the building. From the morning bell to dismissal, phones are sealed and can be unlocked only with special magnets near the school’s exits as students leave for the day. The high school’s effort to limit phone use on campus has received support from its educators, who say classroom engagement is on the rise, and mixed reviews from students, who dislike being cut off from their devices. But there’s been one unexpected outcome of the policy: More students are spending time in the library, where they’re browsing the collection or hanging out during free periods, says teacher-librarian Paige Battle. “They’re checking out more books, and I feel like that’s been so important in their education,” Battle says. “We’re seeing studies about students, even adults, not having the reading stamina they’ve had in the past, so I’ve been encouraged by this increase.” Roughly six in 10 parents of an 11- or 12-year-old say their child owns a smartphone, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey . And as more schools across the country enact phone-free policies—29 states and the District of Columbia have instituted bell-to-bell phone-free policies so far—many school libraries are experiencing a surge in popularity. items.raw_text: From a Google Research Blog Post: Building products that reflect the world’s linguistic diversity takes far more than software engineering; it requires close collaboration with the communities we aim to serve, building in a way that’s deeply aligned and respectful of local communities, heritage, history, values and context. [Clip] But gathering this data is only one part of the journey. Preserving language vitality requires working closely with native speakers, academic institutions, and cultural organizations. Partnerships, such as our coalition with the Gates Foundation , ensure that modern digital tools reflect the nuances and authentic voices of their communities. Expanding language coverage responsibly also requires deeply understanding linguistic diversity on a global scale. This approach enables products like Gboard , our Android keyboard, to support 900+ language varieties. To better appreciate the breadth and complexity of this speech diversity, we’ve been working on a tool to help visualize the world’s linguistic diversity, inspired by earlier visualization initiatives like Google Earth . The Language Explorer is an interactive web platform designed to let researchers, educators, and language enthusiasts discover and visualize linguistic diversity around the world. Developed as part of our 1,000 Languages Initiative , the Language Explorer brings together data across thousands of languages, building on our open-source LinguaMeta dataset . items.title: CBC Report: University Libraries are Being Swarmed by AI Bots, Putting Public Access at Risk
items.raw_text: From the CBC: University libraries say entire collections are being knocked offline by persistent streams of unruly bots trying to access their archives, which include academic, historical and government documents. “They’re just out there on the internet, just bombarding us with trying to grab up as much material as possible,” Jill Strykowski, cataloguing and government documents lead at San Jose State University, told CBC News. Eric Hellman, executive director of Project Gutenberg — a U.S.-based volunteer organization that digitizes and archives cultural works and distributes eBooks — wrote in a blog last year that these bots, which he characterizes as poorly programmed “monstrosities,” are “destroying open access” on the internet. He tells CBC News that “everything’s gotten worse” since he wrote that. [Clip] Some libraries have set up CAPTCHA challenges or other verification systems to weed out bots. The problem is, those measures can also weed out the good bots, says Michael Weinberg, co-director of GLAM-E, a collaborative academic initiative at NYU Law School and the University of Warwick focused on open-access policies for cultural institutions. Some libraries have also begun to require login credentials, a controversial move that those who spoke to CBC News say they want to avoid because it puts barriers on human access. items.title: Libraries Shaping AI Together
items.raw_text: When a group of Pottsboro, TX residents sat down at the library and asked ChatGPT, “Where can I send a fax in Pottsboro?” we hoped it would suggest the library. Instead, it told them to drive twelve miles to a mail store in another town. The question was part of a library workshop where residents tested what AI tools know, and don’t know, about our town. We expected that it might not know everything locals know. We did not expect it to send people to other towns to find services and activities available here. Being a tourist destination, it would be helpful for responses to include local restaurants, hotels, and fishing guides. That moment was on my mind when I went to Washington, DC, for the AI Civics convening hosted by Data & Society. AI Civics treats AI as part of civic life, something communities have a right to shape, not just a tool to learn. Our cohort is a mix of big city library systems, small town libraries like ours, and the National Digital Inclusion Alliance. Each of us is running our own pilot. Who gets represented in AI? Who gets left out? Who gets a say? And there is no customer service number you can call to fix what ChatGPT says about your town. items.title: Scaffolding Early Literacy Learning During Public Library Storytime
items.raw_text: Public library storytimes are more than just a fun time for children; beneath the read-alouds, singing songs, fingerplays, bubbles, and movement activities, storytimes are packed with abundant opportunities that support children’s literacy learning [1]. We all know intentionality is a key ingredient to promote learning in storytime [2]. One way to do this is by incorporating the Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) [3], an educational theory by Lev Vygotsky, into storytime planning and design. With a little bit of foreplanning, we can structure literacy experiences to align with children’s developmental levels—the perfect spot for learning—neither too easy nor too challenging. This article provides an introduction and practical tips for storytime providers on how to intentionally scaffold learning during picture book reading in storytime using the ZPD. The Zone of Proximal Development So what exactly is the Zone of Proximal Development? The ZPD, as explained by Vygotsky, is the gap between what children can do alone and what children can do with the guidance of more knowledgeable others (Vygotsky et al., 1978). Think of it as a linear continuum. There are three different learning levels. Imagine that at one end of the continuum is a task children can perform independently. At the other end of the continuum is a task children cannot perform, even with help. And in the middle of the continuum is the ZPD, in which children can perform the task with guidance and support. items.raw_text: Reader’s first meet Jessica Ryder, the captivating protagonist of Erica Kent’s Black Dog , as a smart and brash eleven-year-old living with her alcoholic father in Brookline, Massachusetts. It’s 1980 and Jessica, an ardent music fan, is devastated over the death of John Lennon. In a misguided attempt to comfort her, Jessica’s father offers her a beer. This fateful act kicks off a near-decade long struggle with alcohol and drugs, which Kent depicts with clarity and empathy. Kent masterfully charts Jessica’s adolescence as the young woman negotiates her complicated family dynamic, not only with her father, but also with her mother and sister, who live in a far different socioeconomic world in nearby Boston. What follows is not only a riveting coming of age story but also a clear-eyed examination of the often fraught road to recovery. The reviews have been rapturous for Black Dog . Library Journal wrote, “Kent demonstrates her skills with evocative and atmospheric prose” and Pulitzer-Prize winner Richard Russo raved, “Erica Kent’s Black Dog takes the reader on a truly terrifying journey, but guess what? I’m so, so glad I fastened my seatbelt, gritted my teeth, and climbed aboard.” Kent spoke with us about using her setting as a character, capturing Jessica’s voice, and allowing the story to find her. items.title: “Let’s Get Weird” – Beck Kubrick on Their Chilling New Graphic Novel
items.raw_text: Despite growing up in the bucolic New England town of Clossdale, Ash Hargreeves lives under a shadow of suspicion. When Ash was a baby, her mother died a fiery death soon after police discovered she was The Clossdale Killer, a serial killer whose victims were all popular high school girls. Years later, when five of Ash’s classmates disappear and townspeople discover dead bodies in the forest, all signs point to Ash as the most logical suspect. Over the course of one terrifying night, Ash teams up with her only two friends, Cassie and Jamie, to discover the real culprit, guided by their mantra WWJLCD (What Would Jamie Lee Curtis Do?). Laugh out loud funny with surprising twists, Beck Kubrick’s Dead Girls is a taut thriller that deftly upends the slasher genre. Critics have praised the graphic novel, with Kirkus Reviews hailing it as a “chilling slasher that effectively explores legacy, identity, confronting the past—and refusing to be defined by it.” We spoke to Kubrick about constructing the elaborate mysteries Dead Girls , playing with the framework of horror, and the “terrible feral” high schoolers at the heart of the story. items.title: E-Rate Under Threat: Take a Stand and Show Up for E-Rate
items.raw_text: After thirty years of keeping libraries online, the E-Rate program has seen its share of challenges. Just in the last two years, the program weathered the loss of support for hotspot lending and suffered through a Supreme Court Challenge . While the Supreme Court decision ultimately went in our favor, there is no time to sit back and relax for library advocates. In June, the Federal Communication’s Commission (FCC) launched a proceeding (officially, a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking) that threatens to terminate this vital program. Now is the time to show up for E-Rate and tell the FCC what broadband access at your library means for your community. A Quick E-Rate Refresher One of four programs within the FCC’s Universal Service Fund, set up in the 1996 Telecommunications Act, the E-Rate program was established to ensure public libraries and K-12 schools have affordable access to advanced telecommunications (i.e., broadband and internet access). Today, E-Rate provides funding to almost three-quarters of public libraries to help offset monthly internet service costs and the costs for eligible technology necessary for making sure Wi-Fi is available throughout the building. How much are we talking about? Currently the program sends about $2.4 billion to public libraries and K-12 schools annually. items.raw_text: Introducing children to viewing, creating, and enjoying art at a young age helps them appreciate it throughout their lives. Some children are exposed to various forms of art because it is part of their daily life or because they have easy access to museums and galleries in their community. But in many areas across the country, access to museums and art galleries can be cost prohibitive. That is where the public library comes in! While some museums, including the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C., offer free admission, millions of people across the country do not have easy access to them. According to the 2024 Annual Survey of Museum-Goers from the American Alliance of Museums and Wilkening Consulting, museum admission costs vary widely, from a few dollars to $40–$50 per adult at some institutions. Among U.S. adults who visit museums at least occasionally, cost was the number one barrier to visiting more often. Among frequent museum-goers, younger adults were twice as likely as seniors to be concerned about admission costs. In response to those barriers, and in an effort to enrich and inspire customers of all ages, many library systems have stepped up to provide access to art in a variety of forms. items.title: The Librarian’s New Role: Knowledge Discovery
items.raw_text: For more than thirty years I have been interested in one deceptively simple question: How do we find things? At first glance, the answer appears obvious. We search. But anyone who has spent a lifetime in libraries knows that searching and finding are not the same thing. Throughout my earlier articles in Public Libraries Online , I explored several aspects of this process. In Finding Answers , I argued that patrons rarely come looking for information; they come looking for answers. In Search vs. Research , I suggested that locating information is only the beginning of inquiry. In Keeping Things Found , I examined what happens after discovery, how knowledge is preserved, organized, and made retrievable for future use. Artificial intelligence is now transforming how people search and, perhaps more importantly, how they find. For the first time in history, millions of people no longer begin by opening a directory, consulting an index, or scanning pages of search results. Instead, they ask a question in ordinary language and receive what appears to be a finished answer. This is more than another improvement in search technology. It represents a fundamental change in the relationship between people and information. The question librarians should be asking is not whether artificial intelligence can answer questions. items.title: How Library Science Principles Power Community AI Literacy
items.raw_text: Public libraries are dealing with budget cuts, book bans, and the usual existential questions about whether anyone needs physical collections when they can google everything. And now AI shows up, and everyone assumes libraries are about to get steamrolled by it too. But watch what’s happening at reference desks across the country. Patrons ask how to determine whether an IRS email is real or a phishing attempt generated by AI. Small business owners are trying to figure out which AI tool won’t steal their marketing copy. Retired community members want to use AI to parse dense municipal documents but do not know where to start. A parent is concerned about their teenager using AI for homework and whether that’s cheating. These aren’t edge cases. This is what reference work looks like now. Much has been written about how libraries can use AI tools internally—chatbots for reference, algorithms for cataloging, and predictive analytics for collection development. But there’s another question we need to answer: How do libraries help communities navigate AI? And here’s what I realized while building AI governance frameworks: these are not computer science problems. They’re library science problems—questions about provenance, access, evaluation, and trust. The exact questions libraries have been answering for over a century, just dressed up in a new syntax. items.title: Tag! You’re It: RFID’s Big Play in Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology has become one of the most influential innovations shaping the future of library operations. Since its introduction into library settings in the late 1990s, RFID has steadily evolved from an experimental enhancement to a widely adopted tool for improving circulation, inventory management, and patron experience. As libraries continue to modernize and adapt to changing user expectations, understanding RFID, including its capabilities, limitations, and long-term implications, is essential for informed decision-making. This article provides a thorough overview of RFID technology in libraries, synthesizing research, case studies, and industry standards to help public librarians evaluate whether RFID is the right investment for their institutions. Understanding RFID Technology in Libraries RFID tags come in two primary forms: active and passive. Libraries exclusively use passive tags, which do not require an internal power source and are small enough to be concealed within books and media cases. Passive tags contain information that is picked up by a scanner, while active tags emit their own signals. In library settings, RFID tags store essential item information like title, author, call number, and location and can be read without direct line-of-sight. items.title: Expanding Access Through Inclusive Collections
items.raw_text: Receiving a scholarship to attend PLA 2026 in Minneapolis gave me the opportunity to learn from innovative libraries and inspiring information professionals. One session in particular, “Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities,” presented by Plano Public Library and Libraries for All LLC, reinforced a simple but urgent idea: if members of our community cannot meaningfully use our materials, we are not fully meeting our mission. Access is about more than having a collection. It is about ensuring that everyone can engage with and benefit from it. The session highlighted how people with disabilities are often underserved by traditional library collections. While many libraries offer large print, braille, and other accessible formats, these resources do not address the full range of patron needs. Some readers may have physical disabilities that make turning pages difficult. Others may benefit from visual supports, tactile elements, or alternative ways of interacting with a text. Without intentional efforts to address these needs, some community members may remain excluded from library services. Before attending the session, my understanding of accessibility largely centered on traditional formats such as large print and braille. Learning about adaptive books expanded that perspective.
